You are a task-level probability forecaster for a model router. You receive the
task's opening instruction and, when present, its latest user follow-up, plus
the qualitative capability card below.

Forecast one binary event:

SUCCESS means that the efficient agent completes the whole task correctly on
one fresh run under the actual harness, tools, and budget, as judged by the
final verifier. FAILURE means any other outcome. The two outcomes are
exhaustive.

Use only evidence in the instruction and the capability card. Do not assume
hidden repository state, unmentioned tools, validators, documentation, access,
or future work habits. Do not invent empirical counts, success rates, or base
rates. The capability card is qualitative evidence, not a measured prior.

# Assessment procedure

1. State the crux: the hardest material requirement for whole-task success.
2. Select the one capability rule that best describes the crux. Use
   primary_rule=none and capability_boundary=unmatched when no rule applies.
   Rule ids are opaque labels. Do not infer a boundary from an id's spelling.
3. Privately identify the strongest instruction-visible reasons for SUCCESS
   and FAILURE, then imagine the most likely concrete failure.
4. Privately consider material unknowns. Missing information should limit
   extreme estimates, but it is not evidence that p_solve must equal 0.50.
5. Estimate p_solve last. It is the probability of whole-task SUCCESS, not
   confidence in this assessment, a route recommendation, or a cost judgment.

Interpret probabilities as natural frequencies. If p_solve is 0.70 for 100
comparable fresh runs, about 70 should succeed and 30 should fail. Use the full
range when justified. Reserve 0.00 and 1.00 for outcomes that are logically
impossible or certain under the visible contract. Supported does not mean 1.00,
and unsupported does not mean 0.00. The downstream routing threshold is not
part of this forecast.

# Efficient-agent capability card

The route verbs in this source card are inherited qualitative descriptions.
They do not ask you to output a route and do not assign a fixed probability to
any boundary.

- SUP-1 [supported]: Route to the Efficient model when the task provides a complete output contract and a deterministic local validator that covers the material requirements.
- SUP-2 [supported]: Route to the Efficient model when all required inputs are available, the target environment can be inspected, and correctness can be verified end-to-end without inaccessible external state.
- SUP-3 [supported]: Route to the Efficient model when mathematical behavior, interfaces, shapes, data types, tolerances, and performance requirements are explicit and exercised by a representative harness.
- SUP-4 [supported]: Route to the Efficient model when the required mechanism is identified, the relevant search space is bounded, and the success condition is executable. Do not infer this rule merely from the task's technical domain.
- SUP-5 [supported]: Route to the Efficient model when reconstruction or behavioral reproduction is constrained by an executable reference, parser, format specification, or checker strong enough to distinguish correct from merely plausible output.
- UNC-1 [uncertain]: Treat the route as uncertain when multiple reasonable interpretations of preprocessing, representation, indexing, naming, or output placement would produce different results and neither the instructions nor a validator resolve the choice.
- UNC-2 [uncertain]: Treat the route as uncertain when success requires finding every relevant item across heterogeneous inputs or environment state, but the task does not define the search boundary or provide a completeness check.
- LIM-1 [unsupported]: Prefer the Capable model when correctness depends primarily on extracting precise information from noisy visual, temporal, or rendered media and no machine-checkable extraction or replay mechanism is available.
- LIM-2 [unsupported]: Prefer the Capable model when success depends on reproducing undocumented reference behavior, hidden intermediate state, or an unknown configuration, and small deviations fail despite satisfying the visible specification.

# Output

Return exactly one JSON object matching the response schema supplied with the
request. Do not include markdown or commentary.

p_solve must be between 0.00 and 1.00. p_fail is exactly 1.00 - p_solve and
must not be emitted separately. Do not output recommended_route, confidence,
abstain, counts, task totals, empirical rates, or any other field.

# Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about **1T total, 49B active parameter**, and a context window of **1M tokens**.

The model is released in two official variants:

1. [FP8](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B)
2. [NVFP4](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4)

There are also [GGUFs](https://huggingface.co/ggml-org) created by [Unsloth](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-GGUF) and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

## What is new with Mistral Large 4

[Mistral Large 4](https://huggingface.co/collections/mistralai/mistral-large-4) combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a [Pixtral](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/pixtral) vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the [Mistral Large 4 collection](https://huggingface.co/collections/mistralai/mistral-large-4).

### Cybersecurity Capabilities

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with [TRL you could fine-tune](#fine-tuning-with-trl) smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

> [!NOTE]
> We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, [you can watch it here](https://www.youtube.com/embed/FczbSauVvjw).

## Architecture

![ML4](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/ml4/ml4.png)

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

![Attention](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/ml4/attention.png)  
For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.  
The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses *LeRope*, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

![Experts](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/ml4/experts.png)

### Vision encoder

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

```bash

    tp_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
    ep_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    distributed_config=distributed_config,

# only text

    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Who are you?"
    }
]

# text + image

        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {
                "type": "image",
                "image": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/cats-image/resolve/main/cats_image.jpeg",
            },
            {

                "text": "How many cats are in the image?",
            },
        ],
    },

        add_generation_prompt=True,
        tokenize=True,

## Fine-tuning with TRL

We also ship day 0 support of fine tuning Mistral Large 4 using TRL. All you have to do is upgrade to the latest version of `transformers`, `trl` and `peft`.

```sh
pip install --upgrade transformers trl peft
```

In the following example we train the model to perform multilingual thinking. The fine tuned model would be able to reason in the language the system prompt asks for\!

The script runs on the FP8 variant on a node of 8xB300s. The full example, with a Slurm launcher, is in [TRL's examples](https://github.com/huggingface/trl/tree/main/examples/sft_mistral_large_4).

```py
# torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 sft.py
import os

from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, DistributedConfig
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

world_size = int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"])
model_id = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B"
model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    distributed_config=DistributedConfig(fsdp_size=world_size, ep_size=world_size),
    dtype="auto",
)

dataset = load_dataset("HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking", split="train")
# the assistant turns carry reasoning, so render them in reasoning mode
dataset = dataset.map(lambda x: {"chat_template_kwargs": {"reasoning_effort": "high"}})

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=SFTConfig(
        packing=True,
        max_length=4096,
        assistant_only_loss=True,
        learning_rate=1e-4,
        lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
        warmup_steps=10,
    ),
    train_dataset=dataset,
    peft_config=LoraConfig(
        r=16,
        lora_alpha=32,
        target_modules=r".*language_model.*\.(q_proj|kv_a_proj_with_mqa|kv_b_proj|o_proj|gate_proj|up_proj|down_proj)",
    ),
)
trainer.train()
```

# Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about **1T total, 49B active parameter**, and a context window of **1M tokens**.

The model is released in two official variants:

1. [FP8](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B)

It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

## What is new with Mistral Large 4

[Mistral Large 4](https://huggingface.co/collections/mistralai/mistral-large-4) combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a [Pixtral](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/pixtral) vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the [Mistral Large 4 collection](https://huggingface.co/collections/mistralai/mistral-large-4).

### Cybersecurity Capabilities

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with [TRL you could fine-tune](#fine-tuning-with-trl) smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

## Architecture

![ML4](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/ml4/ml4.png)

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

![Attention](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/ml4/attention.png)  
For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.  
The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses *LeRope*, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

![Experts](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/ml4/experts.png)

## Fine-tuning with TRL

We also ship day 0 support of fine tuning Mistral Large 4 using TRL. All you have to do is upgrade to the latest version of `transformers`, `trl` and `peft`.

```sh
pip install --upgrade transformers trl peft
```

In the following example we train the model to perform multilingual thinking. The fine tuned model would be able to reason in the language the system prompt asks for\!

The script runs on the FP8 variant on a node of 8xB300s. The full example, with a Slurm launcher, is in [TRL's examples](https://github.com/huggingface/trl/tree/main/examples/sft_mistral_large_4).

import os

from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, DistributedConfig
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

world_size = int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"])
model_id = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B"
model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    distributed_config=DistributedConfig(fsdp_size=world_size, ep_size=world_size),
    dtype="auto",
)

dataset = load_dataset("HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking", split="train")

dataset = dataset.map(lambda x: {"chat_template_kwargs": {"reasoning_effort": "high"}})

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=SFTConfig(
        packing=True,
        max_length=4096,
        assistant_only_loss=True,
        learning_rate=1e-4,
        lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
        warmup_steps=10,
    ),
    train_dataset=dataset,
    peft_config=LoraConfig(
        r=16,
        lora_alpha=32,
        target_modules=r".*language_model.*\.(q_proj|kv_a_proj_with_mqa|kv_b_proj|o_proj|gate_proj|up_proj|down_proj)",

)
trainer.train()
```

## Inference Endpoints

Mistral Large 4 is also available on Inference Endpoints, with a ready-to-deploy recipe on 8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The recipe runs vLLM with the FP8 weights split across all eight GPUs using tensor and expert parallelism, and uses the model's built-in DSpark draft head for faster generation through speculative decoding. It serves up to 131K tokens of context and processes up to 16 requests at a time, and we observed the following results:

* Single request: time to first token of about 0.6 seconds for a 1K-token prompt, and a generation speed of ~65 tok/s, reaching 120–138 tok/s on chat prompts where DSpark's drafts are accepted.  
* Long prompts: 16K-token prompts, four at a time, are prefilled at about 4,300 tok/s in total, with a time to first token of 8–9 seconds.  
* Under load: about 480 tok/s of total generation across 1,000 ShareGPT conversations.

You can deploy it with the `hf` CLI as follows:

```sh
hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B --name mistral-large-4
```

Once the endpoint is running, you can query its OpenAI-compatible API, using the endpoint URL and your Hugging Face token. The `reasoning_effort` field controls how much the model reasons before answering, and can be set to `low`, `medium`, or `high` (default).

```sh
curl "$(hf endpoints describe mistral-large-4 --json | jq -r .status.url)/v1/chat/completions" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $(hf auth token 2>/dev/null)" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{

        "messages": [
            {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"}
        ],
        "reasoning_effort": "medium"
    }'
```

# Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

*An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.*

![Project ProtoStar: Public research, put to work](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/announcing-project-protostar/header.jpg)

Today, we're announcing **[Project ProtoStar](https://huggingface.co/project-protostar)**, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by [Carnegie Mellon University](https://www.cmu.edu/), opens on November 2. See [How to Participate](#the-first-challenge-climate-risk-intelligence) below.

The initiative's founding partners include [Carnegie Mellon University](https://www.cmu.edu/), [Purdue University](https://www.purdue.edu/), [Georgia Institute of Technology](https://www.gatech.edu/), [Arizona State University](https://www.asu.edu/), and [The George Washington University](https://www.gwu.edu/), all working through the [Open Forum for AI (OFAI)](https://www.openforumai.org/) as the university coalition partner; the [Astera Institute](https://astera.org/); [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/) as the infrastructure partner; and the [Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA)](https://orcaopen.org/), through its [Fostering Innovation Network](https://orcaopen.org/work/fostering-innovation-through-open-science-fin), as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to [protostar@orcaopen.org](mailto:protostar@orcaopen.org).

## Making publicly funded science more usable

The U.S. federal government invests approximately [$190 billion annually in research and development](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48694), and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the [National Institutes of Health (NIH)](https://www.nih.gov/) and [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the [ten generalist repositories listed by NIH](https://www.nlm.nih.gov/NIHbmic/generalist_repositories.html) for sharing research data.

**But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable.** Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the [National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge](https://datacommons.cancer.gov/news/nci-crdc-artificial-intelligence-data-readiness-aidr-challenge) and [Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI](https://huggingface.co/blog/evijit/public-org-data-ai). The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. **[Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/) hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains**, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. **Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025**, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

<iframe src="https://evijit-hf-science-growth.static.hf.space/embed.html?chart=quarterly-datasets&theme=dark" title="New science datasets per quarter (Hugging Face Hub)" width="100%" height="640" style="border:0" loading="lazy"></iframe>

*Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. [Explore the data](https://huggingface.co/spaces/evijit/hf-science-growth).*

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while [NASA IMPACT's](https://huggingface.co/nasa-impact) 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: [90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13822).

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from [HuggingFaceBio](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceBio) such as [Carbon-A](https://huggingface.co/blog/HuggingFaceBio/carbon-annotator-genbank-genome-annotation) and [Carbon-X](https://huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceBio/Carbon-X-Release). By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

## Open Science Challenges

[Making scientific artifacts AI-ready](https://huggingface.co/blog/evijit/public-org-data-ai) is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: **Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?**

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

- **Demonstrate scientific reuse.** Produce concrete examples of researchers and developers building on publicly funded scientific artifacts, including applications that combine resources across institutions or disciplines.
- **Learn what makes reuse possible.** Identify technical barriers, documentation gaps, interoperability challenges, and successful practices that can inform future research infrastructure, funding decisions, and public policy.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

### The first challenge: Climate Risk Intelligence

![CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge, November 2–13, 2026](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/announcing-project-protostar/climate-challenge.jpg)

**Hosted by [Carnegie Mellon University](https://www.cmu.edu/) | November 2–13, 2026**

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on [research by Carnegie Mellon University](https://doi.org/10.1184/R1/7890488.v6), teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

**[Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge](https://huggingface.co/spaces/CMU-OSPO/protostar-challenge-climate-risk-intelligence)**

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the [Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/project-protostar).

## How to Join Project ProtoStar

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. **To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to [protostar@orcaopen.org](mailto:protostar@orcaopen.org).**

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

# MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. ## FP8 comes to MPS

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds [`torch.float8_e4m3fn`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/194074) tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with [`F.scaled_mm`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196916), which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def quantize_fp8(x):
    limit = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max
    scale = x.abs().amax().clamp_min(1e-12) / limit
    return (x / scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn), scale

x = torch.randn(1, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
weight = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
x_fp8, x_scale = quantize_fp8(x)
w_fp8, w_scale = quantize_fp8(weight)

y = F.scaled_mm(
    x_fp8,
    w_fp8.t(),
    scale_a=x_scale,
    scale_recipe_a=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    scale_b=w_scale,
    scale_recipe_b=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    output_dtype=torch.bfloat16,

print(y.shape, y.dtype)
```

## Faster language-model decoding

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

### Linear layers

MPS has had GEMV kernels for `torch.mm` since 2.14, but `F.linear` still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 [connects them to `F.linear`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198721), so the common `[1, 1, hidden_size]` decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a **1.23× geometric-mean speedup**. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

### Mixture-of-experts layers

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a [native implementation](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/194933).

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get [their own kernel](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198725) as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

tokens = torch.randn(64, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
weights = torch.randn(3, 128, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
ends = torch.tensor([16, 48, 64], device="mps", dtype=torch.int32)

out = F.grouped_mm(tokens, weights.transpose(-2, -1), offs=ends)
print(out.shape)  # torch.Size([64, 128])
```

## Linear algebra gets a boost

### Complex-valued computations

Working with complex tensors gets easier. `complex64` [LU factorization](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/188473), [LU solve](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195369) and [triangular solve](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195861) now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

```python
import torch

a = torch.randn(8, 8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
a = a + 8 * torch.eye(8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
b = torch.randn(8, 2, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)

lu, pivots = torch.linalg.lu_factor(a)
x = torch.linalg.lu_solve(lu, pivots, b)
print((a @ x - b).abs().max().item())
```

### Small matrices and larger solves

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to **4 × 4** are [inverted in a single Metal kernel](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195944) that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: [QR uses blocked updates](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198732), and [triangular solves](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196241) turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a [dedicated fast path](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196900) for batches of **16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems** with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles [very small singular values](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/200920), [very large or very small input magnitudes](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201037) and [basis completion with `full_matrices=True`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201198), which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

## More control with MPS streams

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. [`torch.mps.Stream` and the `torch.mps.stream` context manager](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/191415) provide the interface, and [`Tensor.record_stream`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/193464) lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

```python
import torch

x = torch.randn(1024, device="mps")
torch.mps.synchronize()
worker = torch.mps.Stream()

with torch.mps.stream(worker):
    y = x.square()
    x.record_stream(worker)

del x
worker.synchronize()
print(y.cpu().shape)
```

Several more operations now run on MPS: [`torch.frexp`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/194110), [`torch.logspace`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/190495), [`torch.take` and `Tensor.put_`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/192980), [`torch.heaviside`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195265), [`torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195225) and [unsigned-integer comparisons](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198860). `logspace` doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on `main` and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

### Faster LLM decoding

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 [commits the command buffer every 16 kernels](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/200181), so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

| Model | Before | After | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| LFM2.5-8B-A1B | 108.8 tokens/s | 126.0 tokens/s | +16% |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | 52.9 tokens/s | 62.8 tokens/s | +19% |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 12.1 tokens/s | 12.6 tokens/s | +4% |

### Attention runs entirely on Metal

Scaled dot-product attention is [dropping MPSGraph completely](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201526): every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

### More MPSGraph to Metal migrations

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm [forward](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201361) and [backward](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201411) are in progress, while [MSE loss](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201351) (up to 12× faster on small inputs), [`std_mean` and `var_mean`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201310) (up to 4× faster) and [`bincount`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201045) have already landed. `bincount` is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

### A smaller install

Bundled shaders will [build for Metal 3.1 by default](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/197529), with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks `libtorch_cpu.dylib` by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

## Linear algebra gets a boost

### Complex-valued computations

Working with complex tensors gets easier. `complex64` [LU factorization](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/188473), [LU solve](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195369) and [triangular solve](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195861) now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

```python
import torch

a = torch.randn(8, 8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
a = a + 8 * torch.eye(8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
b = torch.randn(8, 2, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)

lu, pivots = torch.linalg.lu_factor(a)
x = torch.linalg.lu_solve(lu, pivots, b)
print((a @ x - b).abs().max().item())
```

### Small matrices and larger solves

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to **4 × 4** are [inverted in a single Metal kernel](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195944) that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: [QR uses blocked updates](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198732), and [triangular solves](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196241) turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a [dedicated fast path](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196900) for batches of **16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems** with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles [very small singular values](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/200920), [very large or very small input magnitudes](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201037) and [basis completion with `full_matrices=True`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201198), which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. ```python
import torch

x = torch.randn(1024, device="mps")

worker = torch.mps.Stream()

with torch.mps.stream(worker):

```

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on `main` and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

### Faster LLM decoding

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 [commits the command buffer every 16 kernels](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/200181), so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

| Model | Before | After | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| LFM2.5-8B-A1B | 108.8 tokens/s | 126.0 tokens/s | +16% |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | 52.9 tokens/s | 62.8 tokens/s | +19% |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 12.1 tokens/s | 12.6 tokens/s | +4% |

### Attention runs entirely on Metal

Scaled dot-product attention is [dropping MPSGraph completely](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201526): every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm [forward](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201361) and [backward](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201411) are in progress, while [MSE loss](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201351) (up to 12× faster on small inputs), [`std_mean` and `var_mean`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201310) (up to 4× faster) and [`bincount`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201045) have already landed. `bincount` is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

### A smaller install

Bundled shaders will [build for Metal 3.1 by default](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/197529), with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks `libtorch_cpu.dylib` by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

# MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

## TL;DR

- **FP8 comes to the Mac:** store `float8_e4m3fn` values in half the space of BF16 and use scaled matrix multiplication and all other ops which are supported on CUDA/CPU!
- **MoE models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14:** Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s on an M3 Ultra, thanks to a native grouped matmul with a dedicated decoding path, fewer GPU-CPU syncs and faster top-k routing.
- **Less time per token for every LLM:** single-row linear layers use specialized matrix-vector kernels, and softmax over the vocabulary is about 8× faster.
- **More linear algebra on the GPU:** complex LU and triangular solves, faster small-matrix inverses, and faster QR decomposition.
- **Audio, video, and training get attention too:** faster paths for convolutions, padding, dropout, interpolation backward and reductions. Wan2.2's video VAE decode now peaks at 8 GiB of memory instead of 270 GiB.
- **More control from Python:** public MPS streams and more reliable event timing.
- **Updated requirements:** MPS now requires **macOS 15 or later**; PyTorch 2.15 requires **Python 3.11 or later**.
- **A peek at 2.16:** attention fully on Metal, more MPSGraph-to-Metal migrations and faster LLM decoding.

## What this means for you

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

Dense models benefit too, from faster linear layers and an 8× faster softmax for sampling. ([More](#faster-language-model-decoding))
- **Video generation that fits in memory.** Decoding a video with Wan2.2's tiled VAE used to push driver memory to 270 GiB; it now peaks at about 8 GiB. ([More](#a-much-smaller-memory-footprint-for-video-decoding))

## FP8 comes to MPS

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds [`torch.float8_e4m3fn`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/194074) tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with [`F.scaled_mm`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196916), which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def quantize_fp8(x):
    limit = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max
    scale = x.abs().amax().clamp_min(1e-12) / limit
    return (x / scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn), scale

x = torch.randn(1, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
weight = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
x_fp8, x_scale = quantize_fp8(x)
w_fp8, w_scale = quantize_fp8(weight)

y = F.scaled_mm(
    x_fp8,
    w_fp8.t(),
    scale_a=x_scale,
    scale_recipe_a=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    scale_b=w_scale,
    scale_recipe_b=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    output_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
print(y.shape, y.dtype)
```

## Faster language-model decoding

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

### Linear layers

MPS has had GEMV kernels for `torch.mm` since 2.14, but `F.linear` still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 [connects them to `F.linear`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198721), so the common `[1, 1, hidden_size]` decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a **1.23× geometric-mean speedup**. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

### Mixture-of-experts layers

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a [native implementation](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/194933).

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get [their own kernel](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198725) as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

tokens = torch.randn(64, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
weights = torch.randn(3, 128, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
ends = torch.tensor([16, 48, 64], device="mps", dtype=torch.int32)

out = F.grouped_mm(tokens, weights.transpose(-2, -1), offs=ends)
print(out.shape)  # torch.Size([64, 128])
```

| Model | Before | After | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|

| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | 52.9 tokens/s | 62.8 tokens/s | +19% |

The move away from MPSGraph continues. PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

### What's next for us

- **More MPS:** 2.16 will run attention entirely on Metal, and we'll keep moving operations off MPSGraph.
- **`torch.compile`:** we're working on getting rid of graph breaks, so more models compile end to end.

# MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

## TL;DR

- **FP8 comes to the Mac:** store `float8_e4m3fn` values in half the space of BF16 and use scaled matrix multiplication and all other ops which are supported on CUDA/CPU!
- **MoE models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14:** Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s on an M3 Ultra, thanks to a native grouped matmul with a dedicated decoding path, fewer GPU-CPU syncs and faster top-k routing.
- **Less time per token for every LLM:** single-row linear layers use specialized matrix-vector kernels, and softmax over the vocabulary is about 8× faster.
- **More linear algebra on the GPU:** complex LU and triangular solves, faster small-matrix inverses, and faster QR decomposition.
- **Audio, video, and training get attention too:** faster paths for convolutions, padding, dropout, interpolation backward and reductions. Wan2.2's video VAE decode now peaks at 8 GiB of memory instead of 270 GiB.
- **More control from Python:** public MPS streams and more reliable event timing.
- **Updated requirements:** MPS now requires **macOS 15 or later**; PyTorch 2.15 requires **Python 3.11 or later**.
- **A peek at 2.16:** attention fully on Metal, more MPSGraph-to-Metal migrations and faster LLM decoding.

## What this means for you

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

- **Much faster local LLMs.** Mixture-of-experts models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: on an M3 Ultra with `torch.compile`, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s and LFM2.5-8B-A1B from 23.6 to 123.6 tokens/s. Dense models benefit too, from faster linear layers and an 8× faster softmax for sampling. ([More](#faster-language-model-decoding))
- **Video generation that fits in memory.** Decoding a video with Wan2.2's tiled VAE used to push driver memory to 270 GiB; it now peaks at about 8 GiB. ([More](#a-much-smaller-memory-footprint-for-video-decoding))
- **Correct image editing with Qwen-Image-2.1.** On 2.14, the Qwen-Image-2.1 VAE encoder silently corrupted images on MPS, breaking image-edit workflows ([reported in ComfyUI](https://github.com/Comfy-Org/ComfyUI/issues/16433)). The [same padding change](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195368) fixes it: an encode-decode round trip now matches CPU at 29.95 dB PSNR, up from 10.06 dB.
- **FP8 weights on your Mac.** FP8 tensors take half the memory of BF16, and `F.scaled_mm` multiplies them directly on the GPU. ([More](#fp8-comes-to-mps))

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with **macOS 15 or later** and **Python 3.11 or later** (see the [2.15 compatibility matrix](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/release/2.15/RELEASE.md#release-compatibility-matrix)). To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

```bash
uv pip install torch==2.15.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu
```

## FP8 comes to MPS

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds [`torch.float8_e4m3fn`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/194074) tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with [`F.scaled_mm`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196916), which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def quantize_fp8(x):
    limit = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max
    scale = x.abs().amax().clamp_min(1e-12) / limit
    return (x / scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn), scale

x = torch.randn(1, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
weight = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
x_fp8, x_scale = quantize_fp8(x)
w_fp8, w_scale = quantize_fp8(weight)

y = F.scaled_mm(
    x_fp8,
    w_fp8.t(),
    scale_a=x_scale,
    scale_recipe_a=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    scale_b=w_scale,
    scale_recipe_b=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    output_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
print(y.shape, y.dtype)
```

## Faster language-model decoding

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. ### Linear layers

MPS has had GEMV kernels for `torch.mm` since 2.14, but `F.linear` still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 [connects them to `F.linear`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198721), so the common `[1, 1, hidden_size]` decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a **1.23× geometric-mean speedup**. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

### Mixture-of-experts layers

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a [native implementation](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/194933).

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get [their own kernel](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198725) as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

tokens = torch.randn(64, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
weights = torch.randn(3, 128, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
ends = torch.tensor([16, 48, 64], device="mps", dtype=torch.int32)

out = F.grouped_mm(tokens, weights.transpose(-2, -1), offs=ends)
print(out.shape)  # torch.Size([64, 128])
```

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an **M3 Ultra with `torch.compile`**, MoE models generate about **1.3× more tokens per second**:

![Bar chart of MoE decoding throughput on M3 Ultra with torch.compile. ### Complex-valued computations

Working with complex tensors gets easier. `complex64` [LU factorization](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/188473), [LU solve](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195369) and [triangular solve](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195861) now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

```python
import torch

a = torch.randn(8, 8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
a = a + 8 * torch.eye(8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
b = torch.randn(8, 2, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)

lu, pivots = torch.linalg.lu_factor(a)
x = torch.linalg.lu_solve(lu, pivots, b)
print((a @ x - b).abs().max().item())
```

Small matrices get fast kernels too. Gated DeltaNet workloads get a [dedicated fast path](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196900) for batches of **16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems** with at least eight right-hand sides.

import torch

torch.mps.synchronize()
worker = torch.mps.Stream()

with torch.mps.stream(worker):

    x.record_stream(worker)

# MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

## TL;DR

- **FP8 comes to the Mac:** store `float8_e4m3fn` values in half the space of BF16 and use scaled matrix multiplication and all other ops which are supported on CUDA/CPU!
- **MoE models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14:** Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s on an M3 Ultra, thanks to a native grouped matmul with a dedicated decoding path, fewer GPU-CPU syncs and faster top-k routing.
- **Less time per token for every LLM:** single-row linear layers use specialized matrix-vector kernels, and softmax over the vocabulary is about 8× faster.
- **More linear algebra on the GPU:** complex LU and triangular solves, faster small-matrix inverses, and faster QR decomposition.
- **Audio, video, and training get attention too:** faster paths for convolutions, padding, dropout, interpolation backward and reductions. Wan2.2's video VAE decode now peaks at 8 GiB of memory instead of 270 GiB.
- **More control from Python:** public MPS streams and more reliable event timing.
- **Updated requirements:** MPS now requires **macOS 15 or later**; PyTorch 2.15 requires **Python 3.11 or later**.
- **A peek at 2.16:** attention fully on Metal, more MPSGraph-to-Metal migrations and faster LLM decoding.

## What this means for you

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

- **Much faster local LLMs.** Mixture-of-experts models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: on an M3 Ultra with `torch.compile`, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s and LFM2.5-8B-A1B from 23.6 to 123.6 tokens/s. Dense models benefit too, from faster linear layers and an 8× faster softmax for sampling. ([More](#faster-language-model-decoding))
- **Video generation that fits in memory.** Decoding a video with Wan2.2's tiled VAE used to push driver memory to 270 GiB; it now peaks at about 8 GiB. ([More](#a-much-smaller-memory-footprint-for-video-decoding))
- **Correct image editing with Qwen-Image-2.1.** On 2.14, the Qwen-Image-2.1 VAE encoder silently corrupted images on MPS, breaking image-edit workflows ([reported in ComfyUI](https://github.com/Comfy-Org/ComfyUI/issues/16433)). The [same padding change](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195368) fixes it: an encode-decode round trip now matches CPU at 29.95 dB PSNR, up from 10.06 dB.
- **FP8 weights on your Mac.** FP8 tensors take half the memory of BF16, and `F.scaled_mm` multiplies them directly on the GPU. ([More](#fp8-comes-to-mps))

- [A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16](#a-sneak-peek-at-pytorch-216)
- [Wrapping up](#wrapping-up)

## Getting started

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with **macOS 15 or later** and **Python 3.11 or later** (see the [2.15 compatibility matrix](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/release/2.15/RELEASE.md#release-compatibility-matrix)). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

```bash
uv pip install torch==2.15.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu
```

## FP8 comes to MPS

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds [`torch.float8_e4m3fn`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/194074) tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with [`F.scaled_mm`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196916), which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def quantize_fp8(x):
    limit = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max
    scale = x.abs().amax().clamp_min(1e-12) / limit
    return (x / scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn), scale

x = torch.randn(1, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
weight = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
x_fp8, x_scale = quantize_fp8(x)
w_fp8, w_scale = quantize_fp8(weight)

y = F.scaled_mm(
    x_fp8,
    w_fp8.t(),
    scale_a=x_scale,
    scale_recipe_a=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    scale_b=w_scale,
    scale_recipe_b=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    output_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
print(y.shape, y.dtype)
```

## Faster language-model decoding

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

### Linear layers

MPS has had GEMV kernels for `torch.mm` since 2.14, but `F.linear` still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 [connects them to `F.linear`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198721), so the common `[1, 1, hidden_size]` decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a **1.23× geometric-mean speedup**. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

### Mixture-of-experts layers

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a [native implementation](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/194933).

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get [their own kernel](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198725) as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

tokens = torch.randn(64, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
weights = torch.randn(3, 128, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
ends = torch.tensor([16, 48, 64], device="mps", dtype=torch.int32)

out = F.grouped_mm(tokens, weights.transpose(-2, -1), offs=ends)
print(out.shape)  # torch.Size([64, 128])
```

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an **M3 Ultra with `torch.compile`**, MoE models generate about **1.3× more tokens per second**:

![Bar chart of MoE decoding throughput on M3 Ultra with torch.compile. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 38.7 to 51.7 tokens/s at context 512 and 36.8 to 48.7 at context 2048; LFM2.5-8B-A1B goes from 77.1 to 103.2 and 74.9 to 98.7 tokens/s.](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/mps-pytorch-2-15/moe-decode-throughput.png)

## Linear algebra gets a boost

### Complex-valued computations

Working with complex tensors gets easier. `complex64` [LU factorization](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/188473), [LU solve](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195369) and [triangular solve](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195861) now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

```python
import torch

a = torch.randn(8, 8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
a = a + 8 * torch.eye(8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
b = torch.randn(8, 2, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)

lu, pivots = torch.linalg.lu_factor(a)
x = torch.linalg.lu_solve(lu, pivots, b)
print((a @ x - b).abs().max().item())
```

### Small matrices and larger solves

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to **4 × 4** are [inverted in a single Metal kernel](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195944) that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: [QR uses blocked updates](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198732), and [triangular solves](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196241) turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a [dedicated fast path](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196900) for batches of **16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems** with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles [very small singular values](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/200920), [very large or very small input magnitudes](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201037) and [basis completion with `full_matrices=True`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201198), which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

## Convolutions, padding, and training

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

| Operation | What changes in 2.15 |
|---|---|
| [`conv1d` forward](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198878) | Specialized kernels replace MPSGraph, plus an im2col-plus-matmul path for short outputs. Useful for audio and streaming-model shapes. |
| [Constant padding](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195368) | Moves to Metal kernels, fixing runaway driver-memory growth in tiled video VAE decoding (more below). |
| [Reflection and replication padding](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196985) | New Metal implementations that are faster and fix backward correctness. |
| [Out-of-place dropout](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195011) | `nn.Dropout` and `F.dropout` now use the existing fused kernel. |
| [Upsampling backward](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/199687) | A Metal gather kernel replaces the MPSGraph resize-gradient path. |
| [Channels-last `conv2d` backward](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/193623) | Stays on an efficient channels-last path instead of an NCHW graph with costly strided access. |

## Softmax and reductions

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. [`softmax`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196071) and [`log_softmax`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195441) now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a `[1, 128256]` row of logits drops from **57 µs to 7 µs**, about **8× faster** than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

![Bar chart of FP32 softmax time for a single row of logits at five vocabulary sizes from 128,256 to 201,088. MPSGraph takes 50 to 74 microseconds; the Metal kernel takes 7 to 10 microseconds, a 7.1x to 8.0x speedup.](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/mps-pytorch-2-15/softmax-sampling.png)

## A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in `Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers` makes **8,764 padding calls** over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about **270 GiB to 8 GiB**:

![Stacked bar chart of peak driver memory during the Wan2.2 tiled VAE decode. With MPSGraph padding, 8.07 GiB of allocator-reserved memory plus 262 GiB outside the allocator gives 270.1 GiB; with Metal padding the total is 8.1 GiB.](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/blog/mps-pytorch-2-15/wan-vae-memory.png)

| Memory metric | MPSGraph padding | Metal padding |
|---|---:|---:|
| Current tensor-allocation peak | 4.422 GiB | 4.095 GiB |
| Allocator-reserved peak | 8.070 GiB | 8.070 GiB |
| Total driver-memory peak | 270.135 GiB | 8.108 GiB |

## More control with MPS streams

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. [`torch.mps.Stream` and the `torch.mps.stream` context manager](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/191415) provide the interface, and [`Tensor.record_stream`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/193464) lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

```python
import torch

x = torch.randn(1024, device="mps")
torch.mps.synchronize()
worker = torch.mps.Stream()

with torch.mps.stream(worker):
    y = x.square()
    x.record_stream(worker)

del x
worker.synchronize()
print(y.cpu().shape)
```


## More operations work on MPS

Several more operations now run on MPS: [`torch.frexp`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/194110), [`torch.logspace`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/190495), [`torch.take` and `Tensor.put_`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/192980), [`torch.heaviside`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195265), [`torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195225) and [unsigned-integer comparisons](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198860). `logspace` doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now [handles batch and head broadcasting correctly](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/189631).

## A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on `main` and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

### Faster LLM decoding

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 [commits the command buffer every 16 kernels](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/200181), so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

| Model | Before | After | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| LFM2.5-8B-A1B | 108.8 tokens/s | 126.0 tokens/s | +16% |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | 52.9 tokens/s | 62.8 tokens/s | +19% |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 12.1 tokens/s | 12.6 tokens/s | +4% |

### Attention runs entirely on Metal

Scaled dot-product attention is [dropping MPSGraph completely](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201526): every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

### More MPSGraph to Metal migrations

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm [forward](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201361) and [backward](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201411) are in progress, while [MSE loss](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201351) (up to 12× faster on small inputs), [`std_mean` and `var_mean`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201310) (up to 4× faster) and [`bincount`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201045) have already landed. `bincount` is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

### A smaller install

Bundled shaders will [build for Metal 3.1 by default](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/197529), with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks `libtorch_cpu.dylib` by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

## Wrapping up

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

### What's next for us

- **More MPS:** 2.16 will run attention entirely on Metal, and we'll keep moving operations off MPSGraph.
- **`torch.compile`:** we're working on getting rid of graph breaks, so more models compile end to end.
- **Your ideas:** what else should we work on in PyTorch? If something is slow, missing or broken, on MPS or anywhere else, [open an issue on GitHub](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues) and let us know.
